title: Accretion / dilution
objectives: Answer out loud: Walk me through a merger model.
Answer out loud: All-stock deal: when is it accretive?
Answer out loud: Is accretion good?

steps.body: Determine purchase price (offer price × target shares).
Decide financing mix: cash, new debt, new stock.
Calculate pro forma net income: acquirer NI + target NI − after-tax foregone interest on cash − after-tax interest on new debt − after-tax extra D&A from write-ups + after-tax synergies.
Calculate pro forma shares: acquirer shares + new shares issued.
Pro forma EPS vs. standalone EPS → accretive or dilutive.

blocks.latex: \text{Pro forma EPS} = \frac{\text{NI}_A + \text{NI}_T - \text{after-tax financing costs} + \text{after-tax synergies}}{\text{Acquirer shares} + \text{New shares}}

blocks.title: “Walk me through a merger model.”
blocks.body: **Interview answer:** "Start with the purchase price and how it's financed — cash, debt, or stock. Combine the two companies' net income, subtract the after-tax foregone interest on cash used and the after-tax interest on new debt, subtract any new D&A from asset write-ups, and add after-tax synergies. Divide by the new share count — the acquirer's shares plus any new shares issued. Compare that pro forma EPS to the acquirer's standalone EPS to see if the deal is accretive or dilutive."

blocks.title: What's the shortcut for accretion/dilution?
blocks.teaser: Compare the weighted after-tax cost of financing to the target's earnings yield at the purchase price (target NI ÷ purchase equity value).
blocks.body:
Compare the weighted after-tax cost of financing to the target's earnings yield at the purchase price (target NI ÷ purchase equity value). If what you're buying yields more than what you're paying for the money, the deal is accretive.

**Interview answer:** "If the target's earnings yield at the purchase price is higher than the weighted cost of the cash, debt, and stock used, it's accretive."

blocks.title: In an all-stock deal, when is it accretive?
blocks.teaser: When the acquirer's P/E is higher than the P/E paid for the target.
blocks.body: When the acquirer's P/E is higher than the P/E paid for the target. A high-P/E acquirer's stock is "expensive currency," so it gets more earnings per share issued.

blocks.prompt: In an all-stock deal, when is the deal accretive?

options.text: When the acquirer's P/E is higher than the P/E paid for the target
When the acquirer's P/E is lower than the P/E paid for the target
When the target has more shares than the acquirer
Always, because no debt is used

blocks.explanation: A high-P/E acquirer's stock is "expensive currency": its cost (earnings yield) is below the earnings yield of what it's buying.

blocks.title: Which financing is usually cheapest?
blocks.teaser: Cash (after-tax interest income is low), then debt (after-tax interest), then stock (earnings yield is typically higher).
blocks.body: Cash (after-tax interest income is low), then debt (after-tax interest), then stock (earnings yield is typically higher). This flips if the acquirer has a very high P/E or interest rates are high.

blocks.title: Does accretive mean it's a good deal?
blocks.body:
No. EPS accretion is a short-term accounting measure. A deal can be accretive because it's financed with cheap debt while destroying value — for example, overpaying for a low-growth business. The real test is whether the return on the investment exceeds the cost of capital.

**Interview answer:** "No — accretion just compares financing cost to earnings yield. A deal can be accretive and still overpay. The real question is whether it earns more than the cost of capital."

blocks.title: Why use EPS as the metric?
blocks.teaser: Public company shareholders and boards focus on it, and it's easy to communicate.
blocks.body: Public company shareholders and boards focus on it, and it's easy to communicate. Its weakness is that it ignores risk, the time value of money, and balance sheet strength.
